Character creation is broken down into 15 discrete steps. I know that sounds like a lot, but most of them only take a few seconds to complete. The list is designed to keep you from painting yourself into a corner and having to backtrack. If you go in the order presented in this guide, you shouldn’t have to back up and redo anything.

Don’t worry about dice yet. Now, you are working out who this person is and writing down what they are good at. If you encounter a word in this guide that is confusing, it is probably in the glossary.

One thing to consider - you *can* do all of this on paper, but you don’t have to. I know a lot of you old school players will want to crunch numbers and make a character the *old* way, but 20 Below has a character creator app that can do all of the math for you. It knows every pool and cost and - most importantly - won’t let you go over budget.

## 1. Name

Name your character.

That’s the whole step. It’s cosmetic - nothing else in this book touches it and no rule cares what you picked, but it is the most important step in character creation. I’ve seen one player spend half an hour on this step. Another just rolled some dice for a random name.

## 2. Concept

Your concept is a phrase that tells someone who your character is at a glance. It’s not a sentence. It’s not a paragraph. It’s not your backstory. It’s a quick description that you can express to someone in a couple seconds.

*A burned-out paramedic who just can’t stop running towards the danger.*

*An ex-soldier turned burned-out bodyguard.*

*A retired cat-burglar who sucks at downtime.*

Like your character’s name, there is nothing mechanical at this stage. However, the next two steps hinge on it. Your character’s nature (Step 3) is normally sitting right there in the concept and, many times, your character’s flaws (Step 11) are as well.

## 3. Nature

Your nature is who your character is deep down. It’s what you do when the stakes are high, the pressure is on, and no one is watching them decide. If you lean into your nature during a moment that costs you something, and it will net you a Fate Token. Acting on your character’s core nature will always reward you.

The Nature and Fate system don’t reward you for effectiveness or convenience. It rewards you for consistently playing your Nature.

## Writing Your Own Nature

If none of the premade Natures quite do the trick, you can write your own. The following steps will guide you in the process. They are the same steps that were used to write the premade Natures.

**One or two words.** A label, not a paragraph. If it can’t be read at a glance, it’s too long.

**Write the drive as one sentence.**  This is what your character wants - how they face the world. It’s not a detail from your backstory. It needs to be a driving motivation or goal. “I lost my brother” is backstory. “I don’t let anyone else lose someone they could have saved” is a Nature.

**Make the trigger concrete and repeatable.** A character’s Nature should drive their actions in a very real and palpable way. If you have to ask the GM if your Nature applies in a certain situation, it is probably too vague. Opportunities to exercise your nature should come up often, not once a campaign.

**Your nature doesn’t have to cause problems, but the best ones always do.** A character who blows their cover to make a dramatic entrance is playing to their Nature *and* making a problem for everyone. And really, isn’t that when it is the most fun?

## Premade Natures

**Analyst**: Nothing gets acted on until you understand how it actually works. *Trigger:* Pausing the plan to dig into the mechanism, the pattern or the real cause before moving.

**Avenger**: A wrong doesn’t stay unanswered. *Trigger:* Pursuing payback or justice even when it isn’t the smart move.

**Caregiver**: Other people’s wounds are yours to tend. *Trigger:* Stopping to help, heal or comfort someone at your own expense.

**Charmer**: People are won over, not overpowered. *Trigger:* Turning a hostile or closed-off person into an ally through charm alone.

**Competitor**: Everything is a contest you intend to win. *Trigger:* Turning a task into a competition and pushing past what was needed.

**Daredevil**: The safe option is the boring option. *Trigger:* Taking the reckless, high-stakes move when a safer one was sitting right there.

**Diplomat**: Every conflict has a deal hiding inside it. *Trigger:* Talking two sides down from a fight instead of picking one.

**Enforcer**: A deal is a deal, and someone has to make sure it holds. *Trigger:* Making someone answer for a broken promise or an unpaid debt.

**Fixer**: Every problem has a working solution if you’re clever enough. *Trigger:* Solving a mess through leverage, favors or a clever angle instead of force.

**Ghost**: The less anyone knows about you, the safer everyone is. *Trigger:* Choosing to disappear, stay unseen or erase your trail instead of being known.

**Guardian**: Some things are yours to watch over. *Trigger:* Standing your ground to protect a place, group or thing you’ve claimed.

**Idealist**: The world can be better, and you’re proof it’s worth trying. *Trigger:* Pushing for the principled option when the cynical one is easier.

**Judge**: Right and wrong get named out loud. *Trigger:* Calling out someone’s conduct plainly, even when it’s socially costly.

**Leader**: Someone has to call the shot, so it’s you. *Trigger:* Making the hard call for the group and owning the outcome.

**Loner**: You handle it yourself. *Trigger:* Refusing help, or cutting yourself off from the group, to solve something alone.

**Mentor**: Someone else’s growth matters more than your own credit. *Trigger:* Stepping back so someone else can learn, lead or take the win.

**Opportunist**: Chaos is just an opening nobody has grabbed yet. *Trigger:* Turning someone else’s disaster into your own advantage.

**Perfectionist**: Good enough isn’t. *Trigger:* Redoing it, refusing to ship it, or pushing back on a “good enough” result.

**Protector**: Someone else’s safety comes before yours. *Trigger:* Taking a hit, a risk or a loss meant for someone who can’t fend for themselves.

**Rebel**: Authority is something to test, not obey. *Trigger:* Breaking a rule or defying an order specifically because it was given.

**Showman**: The room should be watching you. *Trigger:* Turning a moment into a performance, at some cost to subtlety or safety.

**Skeptic**: The comfortable answer is usually the wrong one. *Trigger:* Refusing an easy explanation until you’ve checked it yourself.

**Survivor**: Getting through today matters more than looking good doing it. *Trigger:* Choosing the ugly, practical option over the proud one to come out ahead.

**Trickster**: The straight path is boring. *Trigger:* Solving a problem through misdirection, a lie or a bit instead of the obvious approach.

**True Believer**: A cause or a code outranks your own comfort. *Trigger:* Sticking to your code when the easy move would break it.

**Wanderer**: Roots are just something to outrun. *Trigger:* Walking away from a place, group or claim rather than settling into it.

## 4. Attributes

Here comes the part where some people get nervous: numbers.

Every character is described by a series of numbers. The first, and arguably, the most important numbers are your Attributes. I use the words Attributes and Elements interchangeably throughout the book, so don’t get confused by that.

Each of your Attributes starts at 1 for free. You have 20 points to spend across them however you see fit. However, no attribute goes above 10. There is nothing to keep you from specializing in a couple of them and nothing prevents an even spread. Both builds are equally valid. This is the biggest decision in the chapter.

The next step gives you more points for every point you spend here.

**Earth**: flesh and stone. Raw physical force: how strong you are, how hard you hit, how much punishment you can take. Splits into Soak and Potence.

**Air**: breath and weather. Agility, adaptability and sharpness of mind: how fast you react, how well you keep pace when things change, how clearly you think under pressure. Splits into Initiative and Psyche.

**Fire**: drive and hunger. How hard you push, and how much of yourself you put into a confrontation, whether that’s a shouting match or a knife fight. Splits into Ferocity and Presence.

**Water**: tide and undertow. Perception and empathy: how tuned in you are to the world and the people in it, and how much you can weather before it wears you down. Splits into Stamina and Health.

**Moira**: fate, and the threads nobody living gets to see. Luck, destiny, combat instinct, and whatever is otherworldly about you. Splits into Atropos and Klotho.

## 5. Sub-Stat Division

Every element is divided into two Sub-Stats. In this step, you divide the points in a given Element into its Sub-stats. A rating of 7 in Earth gives you 7 points to divide between its Sub-Stats - Soak and Potence.

This step is where your character stops being a cardboard cut-out and starts becoming a person. Two characters with Fire 8 are nothing alike if one dumped it all into Ferocity and the other into Presence. The first will win the fight. The second will make sure there is no fight.

There is nothing preventing you from putting all of your points into one Sub-Stat. However, caution is recommended - a Klotho rating of zero will slow your Ki regeneration to a crawl and you won’t have a lucky number while a Health rating of zero makes it harder to survive and reduces the damage you can take while unconscious to nothing.

Spend wisely.

**Soak** (Earth): your wall against Physical damage: the number an attacker’s dice have to beat to hurt you.

**Potence** (Earth): raw strength. What you can carry, what you can break, who wins when two people push.

**Initiative** (Air): turn order in a fight.

**Psyche** (Air): your wall against Mental attacks, and how many dice you throw making one.

**Ferocity** (Fire): what you add to a Physical strike when you spend Ki to put more behind it.

**Presence** (Fire): your wall against Social attacks, and how many dice you throw making one.

**Stamina** (Water): caps how many Fate Tokens you can hold (three times your Stamina) and how many you can spend in a Scene, and carries you against exhaustion outside a fight.

**Health** (Water): feeds your Health Levels, which is how many hits you can take.

**Atropos** (Moira): feeds Defense, which is how hard you are to touch at all, whether by a blade, a word, or a mind.

**Klotho** (Moira): how much Ki a Short Rest brings back, and your Lucky Number.

## 6. Descriptors

Descriptors add fine details to your character. For every point you spent in a Sub-Stat in step 5, you get a descriptor -  a word or two describing the specific flavor that Sub-Stat brings to your character. These traits are free - they come with the points spent in Sub-Stats. Once you pick them, you can’t change them. There’s no way to buy extras. If you want more, you have to raise the Sub-Stat.

If you put three points in Soak, you get three descriptors for Soak. They should be different ways to shrug off damage rather than three synonyms. A character who is Hardy, Weathered, and Unyielding has a body that holds up, has been through it all, and will not give in.

These descriptors aren’t just decorative and descriptive - they are load bearing and one of the core ways that your Target Number is determined. Every skill defaults to a specific Element. When you want to use a different Element to roll, and you will, your Descriptors are how you do it.

**Player**: I want Ronan to jump up to the top of the building. 
**GM**: That’s acrobatics, so it’s air. That’s a long way, so the difficulty is going to be a difficulty of four. Your air is 1. You have to roll a 5 or less. 
**Player**: Well, Ronan is Mighty. I think he’s strong enough to make that jump. 
**GM**: Yeah. I’ll allow that. Your Earth is 8, so you are aiming for a 12.

Your descriptors are what you point to to justify using an element other than the default. The exchange above is one example of how it works. Intimidation relies on your Presence, so it defaults to fire. However, you can be Intimidating in many ways. For instance:

Sorn *serenely* describes, in exquisite detail, all the ways in which she can inflict pain. She rolls Intimidate using Air.

Ronan picks up a chair and *forcefully* folds it into a ball. He rolls Intimidate using Earth.

Serafina pounds *tirelessly* on a heavy bag for a while and then issues a quiet threat. She rolls Intimidate using Water.

Descriptors aren’t decorative. Or, rather, they aren’t *just* decorative - they are load bearing decorations. Below, you will find some sample descriptors. You can pick from the lists, but are not restricted to them. In fact, players are encouraged to make their own.

**Soak** (Earth): Hardy, Rugged, Stoic, Weathered, Unyielding, Sturdy, Grizzled, Armored, Callused, Thick-Skinned, Leathery, Battle-Worn, Steeled, Resistant, Flinty

**Potence** (Earth): Brawny, Herculean, Mighty, Strapping, Muscular, Titanic, Forceful, Robust, Hulking, Sinewy, Vigorous, Burly, Formidable, Stout, Iron-Armed

**Initiative** (Air): Alert, Reflexive, Twitchy, Vigilant, Quickened, Sharp-Eyed, Instinctive, Keen, Fleet, Snappy, Watchful, Attentive, Sharp, Nimble-Minded, Anticipatory

**Psyche** (Air): Steadfast, Composed, Disciplined, Unshaken, Focused, Resolute, Headstrong, Serene, Level-Headed, Calm, Iron-Willed, Grounded, Unflappable, Determined, Clear-Headed

**Ferocity** (Fire): Brutal, Savage, Relentless, Feral, Merciless, Ruthless, Vicious, Predatory, Fierce, Aggressive, Bloodthirsty, Wrathful, Untamed, Cutthroat, Rabid

**Presence** (Fire): Magnetic, Commanding, Charismatic, Radiant, Imposing, Captivating, Dominant, Alluring, Striking, Charming, Bold, Regal, Magnificent, Unforgettable, Larger-Than-Life

**Stamina** (Water): Indefatigable, Tireless, Enduring, Hardened, Persistent, Unflagging, Dogged, Steady, Untiring, Unwavering, Gritty, Marathon-Bodied, Long-Winded, Driven, Unrelenting

**Health** (Water): Hale, Vital, Resilient, Stalwart, Ironclad, Unbreakable, Durable, Tenacious, Hearty, Sound, Thriving, Hard-to-Kill, Long-Lived, Wholesome, Sturdy-Framed

**Atropos** (Moira): Fated, Untouchable, Uncanny, Ghostly, Warded, Veiled, Overlooked, Passed-Over, Unmarked, Inviolate, Unsevered, Thread-Bound, Unreachable, Spared, Unbroken

**Klotho** (Moira): Lucky, Charmed, Serendipitous, Auspicious, Star-Touched, Timely, Quickening, Renewing, Replenishing, Rekindling, Brimming, Deep-Welled, Spring-Fed, Ever-Spinning, Unspent

## 7. Skills

Skills come in two categories: Everyman Skills and Purchased Skills. 

The GM presents everyone with a list of **Everyman Skills.** These are skills that any functional adult in the setting can do because they live there. They are free. You have your Everyman Skills at Trained.

A modern day campaign may have Athletics, Bureaucracy, Computer Use, Cooking, Driving, Etiquette, First Aid, Literacy, Persuasion, and Streetwise as its Everyman Skills, but it is up to your GM to decide.

You have **15-points** to spend on **Purchased Skills.** Each tier costs 1 point and you climb through them in order, so reaching Trained costs 2 points total, Adept costs 3, Expert 4, and Master 5. Those 15 points won’t go as far as you would like. As with everything else in 20 Below, this is intentional. You can have one skill at Master tier and a couple at Trained, or 5 at Adept, or a wide spread of moderate skill. What you can’t have is everything and choosing makes it interesting.

Every Skill has an Element attached to it. This is the default Element that is used to calculate the Target Number for your roll when using the skill.

**Untrained**: your target number is just the Difficulty, you don’t get to add your attribute.

**Novice**: Attribute plus Difficulty, at Disadvantage.

**Trained**: Attribute plus Difficulty.

**Adept**: Attribute plus Difficulty, with Advantage.

**Expert**: as Adept, and your critical success widens to a roll of 2 or 3.

**Master**: as Expert, and a catastrophic failure gets one reroll. That reroll can only soften the blow to an ordinary failure; it never turns into a success.

## 8. Boons

You have 10 Points to spend on Boons. Boons come in tiers based on how powerful they are - Trivial, Lesser, Greater and Legendary. Trivial boons cost 1 point, Lesser cost 3, Greater cost 5 and Legendary cost 7 point.

A boon is an edge that your character has - a close contact that always answers the phone, a knack for reading the room, ambidexterity. None of them will add dice. They are not quite as powerful as gifts, but they aren’t anything to sneeze at.

Anything leftover from these 10 points rolls over into Discretionary points (Step 12). Don’t try to force the math to avoid waste - there isn’t any.

## 9. Resources

You have **6 points** to spend on Resources. Each Level costs 1 point.

Resources are the material side of your character - money, gear, a place to work out of, people who owe you a favor. If it’s a personal knack, that’s a Boon. If it’s supernatural, that’s a Gift. Resources are just backing.

You’ll notice that buying equipment isn’t part of this step. That’s step 13, and the wait is on purpose. Discretionary points can raise your Wealth, and shopping runs its math against your final Wealth, so Wealth has to stop moving before you can spend against it.

## 10. Gifts

You have **21 points** to spend on Gifts. This is your supernatural budget, and it’s the biggest pool in the chapter.

Every Level of a Gift costs **3 points**. A Gift at Level 3 costs 9. A Gift at Level 5 costs 15. Twenty-one points will buy you one Gift at Level 5 with change left over, or two at Level 3, or seven at Level 1 if you want a character who does a little bit of everything.

Two things bend those numbers.

**Adders** are permanent upgrades to a Gift you already have. A Lesser Adder costs 3 points, a Greater costs 6.

**Limiters** go the other direction. A Limiter is a permanent catch you accept on one of your Gifts, and it knocks a point off every Level of that Gift. Stack as many as you can live with - there’s no ceiling - though the cost per Level never drops below 1.

Limiters are how you afford a Gift you couldn’t otherwise, and you should expect to pay for it at the table. A Limiter that never inconveniences you isn’t worth anything, and your GM will notice.

Because Limiters leave the math uneven, leftover Gifts points don’t evaporate. They convert to Discretionary points at **2:1**.

## 11. Flaws

Flaws are optional. Take them or don’t.

Every Flaw carries its own point value - there’s no formula, so you’ll have to check the Flaw itself. Whatever they’re worth feeds straight into your Discretionary points at step 12. Your GM decides how many you can cash in this way, so ask before you build a character around six of them.

Here’s the part that matters. A Flaw that never costs you anything is worth nothing. If it doesn’t make something harder for this character, in play, at the table, then it isn’t a Flaw - it’s a note in the margin. Flaws are the one place in this game where you get paid up front for trouble you’ve promised to have later. Take the money and have the trouble.

## 12. Discretionary Points

Everyone starts with **10** Discretionary points, flat. Add whatever your Flaws earned you, plus anything left over from your Boons pool at 1:1 and your Gifts pool at 2:1.

Now spend them. The rate gets worse the closer you get to raw power.

**Resources, Skills or Fate Tokens**: 1 point each.

**A Boon point**: 2 points.

**A Gift point**: 4 points.

**An Attribute point**: 8 points.

Fate Tokens have a ceiling. You can’t hold more than three times your Stamina, so buying past that number gets you nothing.

Eight points for a single Attribute point is brutal, and it’s supposed to be. Discretionary points are for finishing a character, not rebuilding one. If you want a higher Attribute, go back to step 4 and buy it there, where it costs you one.

## 13. Equipment

Your Wealth has stopped moving. Go shopping.

Buy your starting gear out of the Weapons & Equipment catalog, against your creation-Wealth. The whole procedure - where creation-Wealth starts, how a Wealth Check runs, and what failing one costs you - lives in Resources, under Wealth at Character Creation.

The short version is that every purchase is a roll. Nothing is automatically free. Failing the roll still gets you the thing - it just costs you Wealth to have insisted on it.

## 14. Figured Characteristics

You don’t buy any of these. They fall out of decisions you already made.

**Health Levels**: 5 plus your Health.

**Poise**: 5 plus your Presence.

**Sanity**: 5 plus your Psyche.

**Defense**: 10 minus your Atropos.

**Movement Rate**: 5 plus your Air, in meters.

**Carrying Capacity**: your Potence squared, times ten, in kilograms.

**Ki**: your strongest Element, plus 8.

Work them out and write them down. If one of these numbers is an unpleasant surprise, this is the last comfortable moment to go back and move some points around.

## 15. Finishing Touches

You start play with **1 Fate Token**. That’s the same as your daily refill, so you’re starting topped up rather than ahead. If you want a cushion, buy more back at step 12 - up to three times your Stamina, which is as many as you can hold at once.

Everything that doesn’t have a number attached goes here. What they look like. How they talk. All the little details that grew out of your step 2 concept while you were busy doing arithmetic.

Then hand the sheet to your GM and let them look it over.

That’s a character. Go play them.
